title: Pescatarian vs Vegetarian: Which Is Better for Your Heart?
meta_description: Pescatarian vs vegetarian after 50: a fair side-by-side on protein, omega-3, B12 and iron, the heart research, and a typical week on each.
excerpt: A fair side-by-side of pescatarian and vegetarian eating after 50: protein, omega-3, B12, iron, the heart research, and a typical week on each.
author: sarah
content:
You've decided to eat less meat, or none at all, and now you're stuck on the next question. Is it better for your heart to go fully vegetarian, or to keep fish on the plate? Let me lay the two side by side, fairly, on the four things that change most after 50: protein, omega-3 fats, vitamin B12 and iron.

The truth is that both patterns can be heart-friendly, and both can go wrong. The difference is mostly in which gaps you have to plan for. The free PescoDial calculator gives you a daily calorie and protein figure built on your age, height and weight.

What each pattern actually includes

A vegetarian eats no meat, poultry or fish. Many still eat eggs and dairy (lacto-ovo vegetarian), and that's the version compared here. A pescatarian eats the same foods plus fish and shellfish. So the only difference on the plate is seafood, and it touches all four nutrients below.

The side-by-side comparison

NutrientVegetarian (with eggs and dairy)Pescatarian
ProteinEggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, tofu, lentils and beans. Doable with planning.Same foods plus fish, high in protein with almost no carbohydrate.
Omega-3 (EPA and DHA)Almost none from food. Flax and walnuts give ALA instead.Fatty fish like salmon, sardines and trout are the main food source.
Vitamin B12Eggs, dairy and fortified foods only. Easy to fall short.Fish and shellfish are rich sources, on top of eggs and dairy.
IronNon-heme iron only (beans, lentils, tofu, greens), which the body absorbs less well.Adds seafood such as oysters, clams and sardines, which carry heme iron, the kind the body absorbs better.
Fiber and saturated fatIn the EPIC-Oxford study, slightly more fiber and slightly less saturated fat than fish eaters.Very close to vegetarians on both in the same study.

Protein: both can get there

Protein matters more after 50 because it helps protect muscle, and muscle is hard to win back.

Fish makes the math simpler. A 3 oz piece of cooked salmon, the American Heart Association's serving size, carries about 19 to 22 g of protein, while a half cup of cooked lentils carries about 9 g. Vegetarians close the gap with eggs (about 6 g in a large one), plain nonfat Greek yogurt (about 17 g in a 6 oz tub) and firm tofu. It works, with a protein food planned into every meal. For the full ranked list, see our guide to pescatarian protein sources. Most of the non-fish foods on it suit vegetarians too.

Omega-3: the clearest difference

This is where the two patterns split the most. The omega-3 fats studied in heart research, EPA and DHA, come mainly from fatty fish. Plant foods like ground flax, chia and walnuts give ALA instead, and the body turns very little ALA into EPA and DHA. The NIH puts the reported conversion rates at less than 15%. The American Heart Association recommends 2 servings of fish a week, particularly fatty fish, and a pescatarian clears that easily. A vegetarian simply won't get much EPA or DHA from food. Which fish carry the most is covered in our guide to fish high in omega-3.

Vitamin B12: the one to plan for

B12 keeps your nerves and red blood cells healthy, and it's only found naturally in animal foods. The adult target is 2.4 mcg a day. Here's what common foods give you, using the NIH's figures:

  • Clams, 3 oz cooked: about 17 mcg, roughly seven times a whole day's target
  • Atlantic salmon, 3 oz cooked: about 2.6 mcg
  • Light tuna, canned in water, 3 oz: about 2.5 mcg
  • Milk, 2%, 1 cup: about 1.3 mcg
  • Egg, 1 large, cooked: about 0.5 mcg

Vegetarians eating eggs and dairy daily can get there, but it's tight. There's a second wrinkle with age. The NIH lists older adults, as well as vegetarians, among those most likely to run low. One reason is atrophic gastritis, found in 8% to 9% of adults 65 and older, which cuts the stomach acid that frees B12 from food. The B12 in fortified foods, such as many breakfast cereals and nutritional yeasts, doesn't need that step. That applies to pescatarians too.

Iron: different for most women after menopause

Iron needs change a lot at this age. Women 19 to 50 need 18 mg a day, but from 51 on the target drops to 8 mg, because monthly blood loss has usually stopped.

The catch for vegetarians is absorption. Plant iron (non-heme) absorbs less well than the heme iron in seafood, and the NIH notes that people who eat vegetarian need 1.8 times as much iron as people who include meat in their diet. Some useful sources, using the NIH's figures:

  • Eastern oysters, 3 oz cooked: about 8 mg
  • Lentils, 1/2 cup cooked: about 3 mg
  • Firm tofu, 1/2 cup: about 3 mg
  • Spinach, 1/2 cup boiled: about 3 mg

A simple habit helps either way: eat plant iron with a vitamin C food, like peppers, tomatoes or citrus, which helps your body absorb it.

What the heart research says, honestly

The biggest long-term comparison is EPIC-Oxford, which followed about 48,000 people in the UK for 18 years. Compared with meat eaters, fish eaters had 13% lower rates of ischaemic heart disease (the kind caused by narrowed arteries) and vegetarians, a group that included vegans, had 22% lower rates. Vegetarians also had 20% higher rates of stroke than meat eaters, mostly the bleeding kind. The authors say more research is needed to confirm this and explain why.

This was an observational study, so it shows links, not proof that the diet caused them. What matters most is the plate you eat every day, not the label.

A note on medicines. This is not for everyone. Talk to your doctor first if you have high blood pressure, kidney or heart problems, diabetes, are pregnant, or take medicine.

  • Statins: either pattern fits a heart-healthy plan. It works alongside your medicine, not in place of it.
  • Blood-pressure medicine: beans, lentils, yogurt and fish all carry potassium, and some of these medicines change how your body handles it. Canned and smoked fish can also be salty. Your pharmacist can tell you what matters for yours.
  • Blood thinners such as warfarin: eating a lot more leafy greens, which many new vegetarians do, changes your vitamin K intake and can affect how the medicine works. Tell whoever manages your dose that your diet is changing.
  • Diabetes medicine: more beans, lentils and grains, or fewer of them, can shift your blood sugar after meals. Some diabetes and stomach-acid medicines can also lower B12 over time, so ask whether yours is one of them.

Any change to a medicine is your prescriber's decision. Ask your doctor or pharmacist before you change anything.

What a typical week looks like on each

A vegetarian week

  • Breakfasts: eggs, Greek yogurt with ground flax, fortified cereal
  • Lunches: lentil soup, a bean and grain bowl, cottage cheese with vegetables
  • Dinners: tofu stir-fry, chickpea curry, spinach omelette, black bean chili
  • The planning job: protein at every meal, daily B12 from eggs, dairy and fortified foods, and vitamin C with beans and greens

A pescatarian week

  • Breakfasts: eggs, Greek yogurt, smoked salmon now and then
  • Lunches: canned salmon or sardines on salad, light tuna and white bean salad, lentil soup
  • Dinners: salmon twice, trout or Atlantic mackerel once, shrimp stir-fry, a bean night
  • The planning job: fatty fish at least twice, low-mercury species from the FDA/EPA "Best Choices" list, and an eye on sodium in canned fish, keeping the day under 2,300 mg

Pick the version you can shop for and cook on a tired Tuesday. The week you keep beats the one you abandon.

When to talk to your doctor

Get checked if you notice any of these, whichever way you eat:

  • Unusual tiredness that doesn't lift, shortness of breath on stairs, or looking paler than usual (possible signs of low iron or anemia)
  • Numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, balance trouble, a sore red tongue, or memory changes (possible signs of low B12)
  • Unusual bruising or bleeding if you take a blood thinner

Chest pain, sudden weakness on one side, or trouble speaking is an emergency. Call 911 or your local emergency number.

The bottom line

Neither pattern wins on every count. Vegetarian eating brought slightly more fiber and less saturated fat in the biggest study. Pescatarian eating makes omega-3s, B12 and well-absorbed iron much easier to get. If you go vegetarian, plan for B12 and protein on purpose. If you go pescatarian, favour fatty, low-mercury fish and watch the salt in canned fish.
